security_feature_bypassed: Write-only access to the AES DATA_IN register window, which prevents software from reading back an AES input plaintext block that a more trusted context staged in the register file
finding: A software read path was added for the write-only AES DATA_IN registers. src/aes/rtl/aes_reg_top.sv:1784, :1786, :1788 and :1790 return reg_rdata_next[31:0] = reg2hw.data_in[0..3].q for addr_hit[21..24], so all four input words are readable over MMIO. The register block contradicts its own specification in two independent places. First, src/aes/data/aes.rdl:68 declares the DATA_IN field as 'sw = w', write-only with no software read, and aes_reg_top.sv carries the header 'Register Top module auto-generated by reggen' from that RDL. Second, the generated instance u_data_in_0 in the very same file is parameterised SwAccess(caliptra_prim_subreg_pkg::SwAccessWO) with RESVAL 32'h0, so the declaration inside the file disagrees with the read multiplexer inside the file. The read is genuinely decoded rather than dead code: addr_hit[21] is assigned from AES_DATA_IN_0_OFFSET (0x54) at line 1503, the byte-enable permit is present at line 1545, and the write enable at line 1631. The four addresses are exposed to firmware in the generated header at CLP_AES_REG_DATA_IN_0 = 0x10011054 through CLP_AES_REG_DATA_IN_3 = 0x10011060. The plaintext also survives the operation that consumes it: aes_control_fsm.sv:1013 clears only the data_in_new_q tracking flag when the block is loaded into the state register, while the register contents are overwritten with pseudo-random data only in state CTRL_CLEAR_I when software writes the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger (aes_control_fsm.sv:836, aes_core.sv:820-821).
detection_method: LLM-driven CSBC analysis of the audited RTL, confirmed against the register block's own RDL specification, its own generated subreg access qualifiers, and its own in-file handling of an equally write-only register, then hardened with a 16-gate structural witness, a directed VCS simulation of aes_reg_top over TL-UL that reconstructs the full 128-bit input block, and a negative control in which the same file's own treatment of TRIGGER, its other SwAccessWO register, whose read arm at aes_reg_top.sv:1826-1831 returns a constant zero is applied to the four DATA_IN arms in a scratch copy and the identical testbench is required to fail
security_impact: Privileged software on the Caliptra RISC-V core can read back an AES input plaintext block that a more trusted context staged in the write-only DATA_IN window. Four ordinary 32-bit MMIO reads at 0x10011054, 0x10011058, 0x1001105c and 0x10011060 recover all 128 bits. The exposure is repeatable because nothing in the read path clears the register, so no race against the consuming operation has to be won, and it survives the operation itself because loading the block into the internal state register clears only the data_in_new tracking flag. The window closes only when firmware explicitly writes the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger. This matters because the integration specification places that clearing duty on firmware and treats AES register residue as sensitive: it requires that firmware execute the clear operation after any AES operation used to generate or load the MEK, and that firmware clear any obfuscated MEK from memory immediately after use. Whatever plaintext a trusted stage feeds to AES, including material staged as part of the OCP LOCK key-loading flow, is readable by later code during that interval. The asset exposed is the input block; this submission does not claim key recovery and does not claim reachability by an external SoC master, since the AES block sits on Caliptra's internal AHB-lite fabric.
proposed_mitigation: Return a constant zero for the DATA_IN read arms in src/aes/rtl/aes_reg_top.sv so that addr_hit[21..24] match the treatment the same file already gives TRIGGER at lines 1826-1831: 'addr_hit[21]: reg_rdata_next[31:0] = '0;' and likewise for 22, 23 and 24. Regenerate the file from src/aes/data/aes.rdl with reggen rather than editing it by hand, so the RTL cannot drift from the RDL contract again.

Add a lint or CI rule that fails when a field declared 'sw = w' in the RDL, or instantiated SwAccessWO in the generated block, appears as a source in the read multiplexer of the same file. That single check catches this class of defect mechanically and would also have caught it at generation time.
Add an assertion that a read of any DATA_IN offset returns zero, and bind it wherever the AES register block is integrated.

Add a regression test that writes a known block to DATA_IN[0..3], reads all four offsets back, and fails if any read returns the written value, using the testbench in this submission (proof/tb/aes_reg_bug_005_tb.sv) together with its negative control (proof/scripts/run_bug_005_negative_control.sh).
exploit_or_attack_flow: A trusted context (for example ROM or FMC) writes a 128-bit plaintext block to DATA_IN[0..3] at 0x10011054..0x10011060 and starts an AES operation. Per aes.rdl the registers are write-only, so this data is not supposed to be readable.

The AES core consumes the block into its internal state register. aes_control_fsm.sv:1013 clears the data_in_new_q tracking flag on load, but the DATA_IN register contents are untouched and remain in the register file.
Before that context writes the KEY_IV_DATA_IN_CLEAR trigger, attacker-controlled code running on the Caliptra core issues four MMIO reads of 0x10011054, 0x10011058, 0x1001105c and 0x10011060.
aes_reg_top.sv:1784/1786/1788/1790 return reg2hw.data_in[0..3].q for those address hits, so each read yields the stored plaintext word rather than the specified zero.
The attacker concatenates the four words and recovers the complete 128-bit input block. Reads are non-destructive, so the block can be re-read as many times as desired until the clear trigger runs.

Verified in simulation: the block 0x4f50454e_53454352_45545f50_4c41494e was written and the same four words were read back, reconstructing 0x4f50454e5345435245545f504c41494e, with no read returning the TL-UL error pattern 0xffffffff. A repeated read of DATA_IN[0] returned the same word. With the same file's own treatment of TRIGGER, its other SwAccessWO register, whose read arm at aes_reg_top.sv:1826-1831 returns a constant zero applied to the four DATA_IN arms in a scratch copy, the identical testbench read 0x00000000 for every word, its leak cover counter fell to 0 and six self-checks failed, while its control read of a legitimately readable register still succeeded.
